title: [New Rx] The Philippines is getting older. What if we treated experience as an asset?
summary: Rather than treating retirement as the expiration of professional value, the Philippines should create markets to harness the accumulated expertise and judgment of older workers as a productive…

blocks.text: The Philippines still thinks of itself as a young country. For decades, our demographic advantage has meant millions of young workers entering the labor force, staffing BPO offices, hospitals, factories and businesses here and abroad.
That advantage will not last forever.

According to the 2024 Census of Population from the Philippine Statistics Authority, 11.42 million Filipinos were already aged 60 or older in 2024, representing 10.2% of the household population. In 2020, the share was only 8.5%. PSA population projections suggest that by 2055, people aged 60 and above could account for about 19.6% of the population. PSA population projections
Almost every discussion of this transition begins with the costs.
More pensions. More chronic diseases. More hospital care. Greater demand for long-term care. Fewer working-age people supporting more retirees.
Those concerns are real. But they also encourage us to think about older people mainly as liabilities on the national balance sheet.
What if we looked at the other side?
A Filipino does not wake up on his 60th birthday having suddenly lost 35 years of accumulated knowledge, professional relationships and judgment.

Consider a 63-year-old physician. She may no longer want hospital nights, a full clinic or a 60-hour workweek. But she could spend 10 hours a week reviewing clinical cases for an international research organization. She could evaluate medical charts, mentor younger physicians, advise a biotechnology company, review drug-safety reports or teach clinical reasoning.

A retired nurse could train virtual-care teams. A former pharmaceutical executive could advise several startups. A retired banker could sit on investment committees. A former regulator could guide companies through systems that took him decades to understand.
What these people possess is difficult to manufacture quickly: judgment, networks, institutional memory, pattern recognition and credibility.
These are not simply social assets. They have economic value.
Some countries have already recognized pieces of this problem.

In Singapore, the government raised the statutory retirement age to 64 and the re-employment age to 69 from July 2026. Eligible employees must be offered re-employment, while programs such as the Senior Employment Credit subsidize employers who retain older workers. Singapore has explicitly described the objective as allowing seniors to remain productive while helping employers retain experienced workers. Singapore Ministry of Manpower on senior re-employment

Japan has gone further in encouraging continued employment. Its latest policy framework sets targets to raise employment among people aged 60 to 69 and expand measures allowing people to work until 70. It also supports job matching through public employment services and the country’s long-established Silver Human Resources Centers. Japan Ministry of Health, Labour and Welfare policy on older workers
These are important models.
But they still largely approach aging through the lens of employment longevity: how to keep older people in work, improve retirement adequacy and reduce the economic pressures of an aging society.
There is a further step the Philippines could explore.
Instead of simply asking how older workers can stay employed longer, ask how their accumulated expertise can be organized, matched with demand, digitized and sold as an economic service.
In other words, treat experience itself as a productive national asset.
Technology now makes that increasingly possible.
A person does not have to choose between a 50-hour workweek and complete retirement. Someone could work five hours a week. Ten hours. One project every quarter. One board meeting a month.

A retired specialist in Manila could review clinical data from the United States. A former executive in Cebu could advise a Singapore company remotely. A Filipino professional who spent 30 years overseas could mentor local entrepreneurs without permanently relocating home.
The objective should not be to force older Filipinos to work longer.

People who have worked for decades deserve pensions, healthcare and the freedom to stop working. Some will have health conditions that make continued employment difficult. Others will simply want retirement.
The goal is productive choice.
Those who remain healthy, capable and interested should not discover that the economy has no use for them unless they return to a conventional full-time job.

The World Health Organization itself cautions against equating aging with loss of productivity or contribution. WHO notes that older people contribute through paid and unpaid work, caregiving, communities and the transfer of knowledge, and argues that spending that enables their participation should be considered an investment rather than simply a cost. WHO on ageing, productivity and contribution
Artificial intelligence may make this opportunity even more important.
AI can summarize a medical chart. But an experienced physician may recognize that it missed the one detail that changes the diagnosis.
AI can generate a regulatory document. Someone who has dealt with regulators for 30 years may know which apparently minor sentence will create problems later.
AI can produce a financial model. An executive who has lived through several crises may recognize assumptions that look mathematically correct but make no commercial sense.
As machines become better at routine work, human judgment may become more valuable, not less.
Healthcare offers an obvious opportunity for the Philippines to test this idea.

The Philippines already had an estimated $4.2-billion healthcare-services outsourcing industry employing around 190,000 people in 2024, according to government industry-promotion materials. Its activities already include clinical support, medical coding, chart abstraction, data management and clinical-trial monitoring. CITEM’s Healthcare Philippines industry report

At the same time, the broader Philippine IT-BPM industry now employs about 1.9 million workers and generates more than $40 billion in annual revenue. IT and Business Process Association of the Philippines

The next evolution of healthcare outsourcing could require less repetitive processing and more clinical judgment, pharmacovigilance, research support, medical review, regulatory affairs, real-world evidence and AI supervision.
That creates an unusual opportunity for older professionals.
A global pharmaceutical company may value a Filipino physician with 30 years of oncology experience for five hours a week more than another full-time junior processor.
A startup may not be able to hire a former hospital CEO, but it could afford her expertise several hours a month.
A young physician entering clinical research may gain enormously from someone who has spent decades navigating hospitals, ethics boards, regulators and professional societies.

Imagine a national marketplace through which Philippine and foreign companies could find retired or semi-retired Filipino doctors, scientists, engineers, accountants, bankers, teachers and executives for fractional assignments.

Professional societies could maintain expert networks. Universities could create senior-fellow pools. BPO companies could develop global expertise-as-a-service businesses. Retired Filipinos abroad could participate remotely.
Instead of exporting only Filipino labor, the Philippines could increasingly export Filipino judgment.

The benefits would extend beyond another paycheck. Older people could maintain income and engagement if they want it. Younger workers gain mentors. SMEs gain access to expertise they could never afford full time. Professional networks are transferred rather than disappearing. Decades of accumulated human capital remain inside the productive economy.
The traditional demographic equation is simple:
More older Filipinos = more healthcare + more pensions + greater dependency.
That equation is incomplete.
There is another side:
More experienced Filipinos = more knowledge + networks + mentorship + productive capacity.
Both are true.

Countries such as Singapore and Japan have institutionalized important parts of senior employment. The Philippines can learn from them, but it can also go further: not simply extending working lives, but deliberately creating markets for what older people know.
That distinction matters because the Philippines is likely to age while it is still trying to become a much wealthier country.

We cannot afford an economy in which millions of people spend four decades accumulating expertise and then, because they cross an arbitrary age threshold, most of that economic capital becomes invisible.
The challenge is not to make Filipinos work forever.
It is to stop treating experience as something that expires at retirement.
An aging population will cost the Philippines money.
The more interesting question is how much value the country is allowing to retire with it. – Rappler.com

Dr. Jaemin Park is an adjunct professor at the University of the Philippines College of Public Health and works across Southeast Asia on healthcare financing, medical innovation, and public sector reform.
